title: Occurrence, Preparation, and Properties of Sulfur
lead: Sulfur is found in elemental deposits, in sulfide and sulfate minerals and in natural and volcanic gases. The Frasch process brings it up from underground deposits, and as a nonmetal of group 16 it oxidizes metals and is itself oxidized by more electronegative nonmetals.
objectives: Describe the properties, preparation, and uses of sulfur
summary_html: Sulfur (group 16) reacts with almost all metals and readily forms the sulfide ion, S2−, in which it has as oxidation state of 2−. Sulfur reacts with most nonmetals.

exercises.prompt: Explain why hydrogen sulfide is a gas at room temperature, whereas water, which has a lower molecular mass, is a liquid.

answer.solution: Water is a liquid because its molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds, while hydrogen sulfide molecules attract one another only by much weaker forces. Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom such as oxygen. Oxygen (electronegativity 3.5) makes the O–H bonds very polar, and each H<sub>2</sub>O molecule hydrogen bonds strongly to its neighbors through its lone pairs and its partly positive hydrogen atoms. Sulfur is larger and less electronegative (2.5, close to hydrogen at 2.1), so the S–H bonds are only slightly polar and H<sub>2</sub>S forms essentially no hydrogen bonds; only dispersion forces and weak dipole-dipole attractions hold its molecules together. Although H<sub>2</sub>S has the higher molar mass, 34 g/mol against 18 g/mol, far less energy is needed to separate its molecules, so it boils at about −60 °C, whereas water boils at 100 °C.

exercises.prompt: Give the hybridization and oxidation state for sulfur in SO<sub>2</sub>, in SO<sub>3</sub>, and in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
Which is the stronger acid, NaHSO<sub>3</sub> or NaHSO<sub>4</sub>?

answer.solution: NaHSO4 is the stronger acid. Each salt supplies its anion as the acid: ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{−}$ from NaHSO4 and ${\text{HSO}}_{3}{}^{−}$ from NaHSO3. In ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{−}$ the sulfur atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and has an oxidation state of +6; in ${\text{HSO}}_{3}{}^{−}$ it is bonded to three oxygen atoms and has an oxidation state of +4. For oxyacids of the same central atom, acid strength increases with the number of oxygen atoms bonded to it, because the extra electronegative oxygen atoms and the higher oxidation state draw electron density away from the O–H bond, making it more polar and the proton easier to lose, and they also spread the negative charge of the conjugate base. ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{−}$ has Ka = 1.2 × 10−2, whereas ${\text{HSO}}_{3}{}^{−}$ has Ka = 6.4 × 10−8.

exercises.prompt: Determine the oxidation state of sulfur in SF<sub>6</sub>, SO<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>, and KHS.

answer.solution: SF<sub>6</sub>: S = 6+; SO<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>: S = 6+; KHS: S = 2−

exercises.prompt: Which is a stronger acid, sulfurous acid or sulfuric acid? Why?

answer.solution: Sulfuric acid, H2SO4, is the stronger acid; it is a strong acid, while sulfurous acid, H2SO3, is weak (Ka1 = 1.6 × 10−2). In sulfuric acid the sulfur atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, two of them OH groups, and has an oxidation state of +6; in sulfurous acid it is bonded to three oxygen atoms, two of them OH groups, and has an oxidation state of +4. Each additional oxygen atom bonded to the central atom, together with the higher oxidation state of sulfur, draws more electron density away from the O–H bonds. Those bonds become more polar, so the hydrogen ions are lost more easily, and the negative charge left on the anion is spread over more oxygen atoms, which stabilizes ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{−}$ more than ${\text{HSO}}_{3}{}^{−}$. For this reason H2SO4 ionizes completely in its first step in water, while H2SO3 ionizes only partly.

exercises.prompt: Oxygen forms double bonds in O<sub>2</sub>, but sulfur forms single bonds in S<sub>8</sub>. Why?

answer.solution: Sulfur is able to form double bonds only at high temperatures (substantially endothermic conditions), which is not the case for oxygen.

exercises.prompt: Write two balanced chemical equations in which sulfuric acid acts as an oxidizing agent.

answer.solution: There are many possible answers including: $\text{Cu}(s)+2{\text{H}}_{2}{\text{SO}}_{4}(l)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{CuSO}}_{4}(aq)+{\text{SO}}_{2}(g)+2{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)$ and $\text{C}(s)+2{\text{H}}_{2}{\text{SO}}_{4}(l)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{CO}}_{2}(g)+2{\text{SO}}_{2}(g)+2{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)$

exercises.prompt: Explain why sulfuric acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, which is a covalent molecule, dissolves in water and produces a solution that contains ions.

answer.solution: Sulfuric acid dissolves and forms ions because it is a strong acid that transfers a proton to water. Its molecule contains two highly polar O–H bonds: the sulfur atom, in the +6 oxidation state and bonded to four electronegative oxygen atoms, draws electron density away from them. When the molecule dissolves it hydrogen bonds to water, and a water molecule, acting as a base, takes a proton from an O–H group. The first ionization is complete: $${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{SO}}_{4}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{+}(aq)+{\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{−}(aq)$$ The hydrogen sulfate ion then ionizes partly in a second step: $${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{−}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\;\rightleftharpoons \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{+}(aq)+{\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{2−}(aq)$$ The covalent molecules thus become hydronium ions, hydrogen sulfate ions and some sulfate ions, which are stabilized by hydration, so the solution conducts electricity.

exercises.prompt: How many grams of Epsom salts (MgSO<sub>4</sub>⋅7H<sub>2</sub>O) will form from 5.0 kg of magnesium?

answer.hint: Convert the mass of magnesium to moles with its molar mass, use the one-to-one ratio of Mg to MgSO<sub>4</sub>⋅7H<sub>2</sub>O, and convert moles of the hydrate to grams with its molar mass.
